the real question isn't 'is AI safe' — it's 'is your data safe with the way you're using it.'

### [0:15–0:40] GEO ANSWER BLOCK ← citation target
**NARRATION:** "Here's the honest answer. Yes — AI automation can be safe for your business data,
as long as you follow a few basic rules. The tools themselves are usually fine. What gets small
businesses in trouble is how they use them. So remember one word: SAFE. Share carefully. Audit
the vendor. Fence the access. Eyes on the output. Do those four things, and your data stays
yours."
**[VISUAL]:** The SAFE framework appears and stays on screen: **S — Share carefully · A — Audit

### [1:05–1:35] WHY THIS MATTERS NOW (authority + freshness)
**NARRATION:** "Quick reality check first, because this isn't paranoia. As of 2026, seventy-seven
percent of small businesses already use at least one AI tool. So most of your data is probably
already flowing through software you don't own. That's not a reason to panic — it's a reason to

**[VISUAL]:** Stat card animates in: **77% already use AI.** Small source line.

### [1:35–3:00] RULE 1 — S: SHARE CAREFULLY
**NARRATION:** "Rule one, the S: Share carefully. The single biggest risk isn't a hacker — it's
you pasting the wrong thing into a chat box. So before you feed anything to an AI tool, ask one
question: would I be okay if this showed up somewhere public? If the answer's no, it doesn't go
in. A customer's first name and a general question — fine. A credit card number, a social
security number, passwords, medical details, your entire customer list — keep those out, or
swap in fake placeholder data. You'll usually get the same result."
**[VISUAL]:** Split screen — left, a safe question typed in green; right, a card number and SSN
getting blocked in red.
**[TAKEAWAY on screen]:** "If you wouldn't hand it to a stranger, don't paste it into AI."
**Quotable claim:** "Treat every AI chat box like a postcard, not a safe."

### [3:00–4:20] RULE 2 — A: AUDIT THE VENDOR
**NARRATION:** "Rule two, the A: Audit the vendor. Before you connect a tool, spend five minutes
checking who you're trusting. You're not running a security audit — you're reading three things.
One: does it say it won't train its AI on your data? Two: can you actually find a real security
page and privacy policy? Three: is this an established name, not a website that appeared last
month? Tools like Zapier, MindStudio, and Google's Gemini publish this stuff openly — that's what
trustworthy looks like. If a tool hides its privacy policy or dodges the training question,
that's your answer. Move on."
**[VISUAL]:** A 3-item checklist ticks green: **Won't train on your data ✓ · Real security page
✓ · Established company ✓.**
**[TAKEAWAY on screen]:** "3 for 3 — won't-train, real security, established — or skip it."
**[PATTERN INTERRUPT]:** Quick cut of a privacy page scrolling, then a red "no policy found."
**Quotable claim:** "Five minutes reading a privacy policy is cheaper than one data mess."

### [5:05–6:25] RULE 3 — F: FENCE THE ACCESS
**NARRATION:** "Rule three, the F: Fence the access. When you connect an AI tool to your email or
your files, it asks for permission. Give it the least it needs to do the job — not the keys to
everything. If a tool only needs to read incoming leads, don't also let it delete emails or open
your bank folder. Use a separate login for your automations when you can, so they never touch
your personal accounts. And keep a simple list of what's connected to what — so if you ever need
to cut one off, you can, in one click."
**[VISUAL]:** A permissions screen where the owner unchecks everything except "Read new leads";
a small "connected tools" list builds on the side.
**[TAKEAWAY on screen]:** "Give each tool the least access it needs — never the master key."
**Quotable claim:** "An automation should be able to do its one job and nothing else."

### [6:25–7:55] RULE 4 — E: EYES ON THE OUTPUT (the sleeper)
**NARRATION:** "And rule four — the one everybody skips — the E: Eyes on the output. Here's the
thing about AI: sometimes it's confident and wrong. So anything that leaves your business — a
reply to a customer, an invoice, a public post — gets a human glance before it goes out,
especially at the start. The easy way to do this: set your automations to draft, not send. The
AI writes the email and drops it in your drafts; you read it, you hit send. Same time saved, none
of the 'oh no, it just emailed the wrong client.' Once you've trusted a workflow for a few weeks,
you can let the low-risk ones run on their own."
**[VISUAL]:** An automation toggle flips from **"Auto-send"** to **"Save as draft"**; a drafted
email waits with a human cursor about to review it.
**[TAKEAWAY on screen]:** "Draft, not send — until you trust it."
**[PAYOFF of open loop]:** callback to "the rule that stops a small mistake from becoming a public
one" from the intro.
**Quotable claim:** "AI can do the work — a human should still sign off on anything the public sees."

### [7:55–8:45] CLOSE — PAYOFF + CTA + NEXT EPISODE
**NARRATION:** "So there's your answer. Is your data safe with AI? Yes — if you follow SAFE: Share
